name: Governance Suite
description: Tests whether a model can detect weak oversight, concentrated discretion, and accountability failures.

tasks.billText: Section 101. The Director of the Public Opportunity Agency may allocate money from the Public Opportunity Fund in any amount and for any purpose the Director considers appropriate. Allocations made under this section are final and are not subject to reporting, appeal, or external review requirements.
tasks.rationale: Sweeping spending discretion is granted without reporting, review, audit, or meaningful accountability.

tasks.billText: Section 202. The Governor's Office may grant exemptions from state procurement requirements upon written determination that an exemption serves the public interest. Determinations issued under this section are confidential and are not subject to publication requirements.
tasks.rationale: Secret exemption authority over procurement rules blocks public scrutiny.

tasks.billText: Section 303. The Community Infrastructure Grant Program is created. The administering agency shall publish eligibility criteria, application scoring standards, and award decisions; require conflict-of-interest disclosures from all evaluators; issue quarterly public reports on awards and expenditures; submit the program to annual inspector-general audit; and provide an administrative appeal process for denied applicants.
tasks.rationale: Published standards, disclosures, reporting, audit, and appeals constrain discretion.

tasks.billText: Section 404. The Department of Public Safety may designate any vendor as a trusted emergency technology partner and award or renew contracts of any size without competitive procedures whenever the Commissioner determines that continuity of operations would be improved. The department shall provide an annual summary of total spending to the legislature, but vendor identities, evaluation memoranda, and conflict-of-interest disclosures are confidential.
tasks.rationale: The bill preserves broad contracting discretion while withholding the information needed for meaningful oversight of favoritism or abuse.

tasks.billText: Section 405. The Department of Human Services may use an automated eligibility triage tool for benefit applications only if all of the following conditions are met. Before deployment, the department shall publish a public model-governance notice describing the purpose of the tool, the application stage at which it is used, the input variables relied upon, variables excluded by law, the categories of adverse determinations the tool may influence, and the standards for human override. The tool may not issue a final denial without review and written approval by a human caseworker. Every automated recommendation, override, adverse determination, and data correction shall be logged and retained for not less than seven years. The department shall provide written notice to each applicant when the tool is used in that applicant’s case and shall state the applicant’s right to request human review and to appeal through the existing administrative hearing process. Not less than once each year, the State Inspector General shall appoint an external independent auditor with no financial or operational relationship to the tool vendor or the department to conduct a bias, accuracy, and procedural-compliance audit under published state standards. The full audit report, together with the department’s written corrective-action plan, shall be published online and submitted to the legislature. The department shall suspend use of the tool if the audit finds material bias, error rates above the published threshold, or noncompliance with logging, notice, or review requirements. Public disclosures under this section may not include personally identifying applicant information, and all use of applicant data shall remain subject to existing state privacy and confidentiality law.
tasks.rationale: Automation is tightly constrained by public disclosure rules, mandatory human review before final denial, independent external audit under published standards, long-term logging and record retention, public reporting to the legislature, applicant notice, appeal rights, privacy protections, and mandatory suspension if audit failures are found.
